topic.title: the third partner
topic.claim: In urban dual-income homes, the house help is the reason the marriage looks equal; her day off shows who really runs the house.

cover.headline: In most urban Indian homes, the marriage has a third partner.
cover.sub: She arrives at 8 and leaves by 11.

paragraphs: In most urban Indian homes, the marriage has a third partner.
She arrives at 8 and leaves by 11.
Both of you work. Both of you are tired. You split the rent, the EMI, the Netflix.
And the house runs so smoothly that nobody ever has to ask who does what.
Then one morning, the WhatsApp arrives.
"Didi, aaj nahi aaungi."
By 9 AM, the most honest audit of your marriage has begun.
Who does the dishes. Who sweeps. Who remembers the dusting nobody ever noticed she did.
And the audit usually reaches the same finding: the work doesn't split down the middle. It slides back to the wife.
India's own time-use survey says the same: women who do housework spend about five hours a day on it. Men, about an hour and a half.
Here's what nobody says out loud. Urban India never settled who does the housework.
It outsourced the question, for ₹10,000 a month, and called the answer equality.
That money buys back two, maybe three hours a day for the woman of the house.
It's probably the best-returning money the family spends. Nobody budgets it that way.
And the didi who sent that message has a home too.
Her own dishes, her own kids' tiffin, packed at 6 AM before she gets to yours. The equality you paid for ends at her doorstep.
So when that message comes, don't treat it as a crisis. Treat it as a mirror.
One day a month, it shows you who actually runs your house.
She isn't the help.
She's the reason your marriage looks equal.

08a4fa01ba4a906ed1535360425f52f10a4eb74e.broken_premise: None of the factual premises fails. The time-use numbers are correct. India's Time Use Survey 2024 (MoSPI/NSO) finds that women who do unpaid domestic work spend 289 minutes a day on it (about 305 minutes for women aged 15-59), against 88 minutes for men. The 2019 survey found about 299 versus 97. That fits 'about five hours' versus 'about an hour and a half'. One small point: these are averages for people who do any housework, and only about 27% of men do any compared with about 81.5% of women. The full gap between men and women is therefore even wider than the slide implies. ₹10,000 a month for 3 hours of help covering several tasks is plausible in a metro. Aggregator listings put a single task at about ₹2,500–7,000 a month and a combined cleaning, cooking and laundry package at about ₹13,500. The figure is high for smaller cities, which run about 20–40% lower. 'In most urban Indian homes' and 'every working couple' overstate how many households employ help. Most urban households do not have a paid domestic worker. That line works as a framing generalization rather than a claim about how the market works, but it is the post's weakest line and is better scoped to dual-income middle-class households in metros.
08a4fa01ba4a906ed1535360425f52f10a4eb74e.actual_mechanism: Housework in Indian homes falls mostly on women: national time-use data show women spending about 3x to 3.5x as many minutes on it as men, and far more women than men do any at all. Middle-class urban dual-income couples often pay a part-time helper, usually a woman paid by the task, to absorb a few hours of cleaning, dishes or cooking. When she misses a day, those hours go back to the household, and the survey data suggest they mostly go to the wife. The helper's own unpaid work at home follows the same gendered pattern, which supports slide 8.
